title: Open-source DRAM-cell library on US foundry PDKs
idea: Worsen: keep storage-cell know-how locked inside three companies. Flip: spend $1M over 24 months designing, taping out and publishing open-source eDRAM and gain cells (thick-oxide 3T, MIM 1T1C) on SkyWater 130 and 22FDX PDKs with measured retention data, so any US chip team can add dense memory.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supply diversification; lowers the entry cost for new memory makers.
note: Clearly executable on open PDKs; ecosystem value, not a step change in cost per bit.

title: Pinned-photodiode buried node borrowed from image-sensor foundries
idea: MAGNIFY retention by holding the bit in a fully depleted, surface-pinned buried n-well (a CIS pinned photodiode kept dark, dark current ~1-10 e-/s) with a transfer gate and source-follower readout like a global-shutter pixel memory, taped out on a commercial CIS MPW.
why: Retention of seconds to minutes at ~2,000 e- cuts refresh energy and bandwidth >100x (fact 3) on a known foundry process; ~0.5-1 um2 cells suit low-power embedded tiers.
note: CIS pinned node gives long retention on a known process; large cells, niche.

title: Redox pseudocapacitor nanocell replaces 70:1 pillar with planar charge sponge
idea: Effect walk: Faradaic surface redox (pseudocapacitance). Replace the dielectric capacitor with a 5-nm hydrous RuO2 or Ti3C2 MXene film against a nanometre solid proton conductor; fast surface redox stores ~100-1000 uF/cm2 versus ~7 uF/cm2 for ZrO2, so a flat 30x30 nm pad holds ~4-5 fF at 0.5 V.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) with no AR 60-75 etch, removing the deep-etch/deposition module (~30-50% of capacitor cost); risks are self-discharge and whether surface redox keeps up at ns timescales.
note: Planar 4-5 fF pad removes the pillar; pseudocap kinetics are ms-scale and self-discharge is high.

title: Po: a wafer is a napkin — remote-epitaxy peel-and-stack floating-body tiers
idea: Po: a wafer is a napkin you can peel. Extracted: grow 50 nm single-crystal Si films by remote epitaxy through graphene on a reusable donor wafer, peel and laminate 64 of them; each membrane carries capacitor-less floating-body cells defined by one imprint step, and each donor is reused ~100 times.
why: Avoids Si/SiGe superlattice epitaxy and high-AR etch and amortises crystal cost over 100 reuses; 64 tiers with no EUV aims at ~100x $/GB. Trade-offs: bonding yield and tier-to-tier alignment.
note: Reusable-donor peel-and-stack could slash $/GB; doubt: remote epitaxy of nonpolar Si and 64-tier alignment yield.

title: Short-retention cells matched to ephemeral AI tensors
idea: Combine compiler-known tensor lifetimes with deliberately cheap short-retention cells: activations, KV-cache pages and gradients that are overwritten within 50 ms go to a pool whose cells retain only ~100 ms worst case and are never refreshed. A runtime time-to-live tag per page rewrites or evicts data before expiry, so refresh disappears and the capacitor can be ~3x smaller.
why: Zero refresh power for the AI-dominant data class, and a smaller Cs (fact 1) allows lower AR and a cheaper process.
note: Compiler TTL plus unrefreshed short-retention pool; provable on FPGA with refresh disabled.

title: Sell retention-fallout dies as permanent fast-refresh DDR5 SKUs
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): standard controllers only. Dies that miss 64 ms retention because of a weak-cell tail are fused to always report the hot-temperature refresh-rate code (2x or 4x refresh) in the existing MR4 register, so stock controllers refresh them faster, and they sell at a discount into capacity-hungry, bandwidth-tolerant tiers such as CXL expanders and inference KV-cache.
why: Recovers a few percent of wafer output now scrapped or downbinned, raising usable bit supply immediately with zero capex (cost per bit, supply).
note: Uses existing MR4 refresh-rate code; modest supply gain.

title: Po: memory printed like a newspaper — roll-to-roll nanoimprinted oxide cells
idea: Po: memory is printed like a newspaper. Extracted: roll-to-roll nanoimprint 50 nm features onto steel or polyimide foil, with spatial-ALD oxide channels and planar capacitors, making 1T1C arrays on a 1 m web; the slower cells sit behind a small silicon cache.
why: Processed DRAM silicon costs on the order of $100k/m2 vs ~$10-50/m2 for R2R, so even at ~17x lower density cost per bit can fall 100x+. Overlay accuracy on a moving web is the key risk.
note: Huge area-cost leverage if 50 nm overlay on a moving web works; that is far from shown.

title: Swap layer-by-layer 3D stacking for rolling one patterned membrane
idea: Pattern one planar layer of thin-film gain cells with DUV on a strained SiNx bilayer, release it, and let the built-in strain roll it into a 20-winding tube. Each winding becomes a memory tier, and the tiers connect through edge contacts along the roll axis.
why: Gives 20 tiers from one deposition and patterning sequence (fact 2), so cost does not grow with the tier count, and no EUV is used (fact 4).
note: 20 tiers from one patterning would collapse 3D cost; dense edge interconnect across windings and alignment are the doubt.

title: Optane's crosspoint kept, PCM swapped for selector-gated capacitor
idea: Optane died largely on cost and PCM endurance, but its stacked crosspoint and OTS selector worked. Place a tiny MIM capacitor in series with the OTS at each crosspoint: the selector's threshold snap acts as a transistor-free access device, turning the array into a refreshed 4F2 multi-deck DRAM.
why: 4F2 per deck with stackable decks and no lateral transistor (Fact 2); reuses idle chalcogenide PVD tooling. Risk: OTS sub-threshold leakage must reach ~fA.
note: Transistor-free multi-deck DRAM; OTS off-leakage needs fA-level, orders below demonstrated, and holding-current behavior complicates writes.

title: Eliminate storage-node lithography: transistors electroplate their own capacitor towers
idea: Eliminate the storage-node mask and etch: after building the access transistors, immerse the wafer in a plating bath and turn on every wordline so each working transistor's drain contact sources current and plates its own Ni/Ru nanotower; then add ALD dielectric (N2 purge) and top plate. No argon-sputtered seed is needed because the drains are the seeds.
why: Self-aligned capacitor with no litho layer and no etch (fact 4); towers reach AR 100+ by plating time (fact 1); dead transistors grow no node, giving a built-in yield screen; risk is plating uniformity across billions of sites.
note: Transistors plate their own nodes: self-aligned, mask-free, built-in yield screen; free-standing AR-100 towers will lean and collapse.

title: Eliminate the 64-ms retention spec: ephemeral sub-femtofarad cells for transient tensors
idea: Eliminate the assumption that every bit must survive 64 ms: build a memory class whose storage node is a planar ~0.5 fF capacitor with no pillar and ~100 us retention, used only for AI activations, KV-cache spill and gradients that are overwritten within microseconds; the controller tags allocations by lifetime and never refreshes them.
why: Removes the AR 60-75 pillar (facts 1, 4) for a large share of AI traffic; ~2-3x cheaper per bit for the ephemeral tier with zero refresh energy (fact 3).
note: Lifetime-matched no-refresh tier for AI transients; similar to refresh-skipping eDRAM for DNNs.

title: Fifty-electron bit read by repeated non-destructive skipper sampling
idea: MINIFY the stored charge ~600x (from ~30,000 e- to ~50 e-): the storage node is a ~0.01 fF floating diffusion with no capacitor, and a per-subarray skipper-CCD-style floating-gate amplifier shuttles the packet under its sense gate N=16 times, averaging read noise below 1 e- rms before write-back.
why: Deletes the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and the AR 60-75:1 etch; cell heads toward 4F2 and write CV2 energy falls ~100x. Only viable if node leakage is pushed to ~1e-21 A (pair with a wide-gap or pinned node).
note: ~600x less charge kills the capacitor wall; doubts: 1e-21 A node leakage and 16 skipper samples within DRAM latency.
